strengths: Well-motivated metric: VIG provides a principled, interpretable measure of visual contribution with clear mathematical formulation and proper theoretical grounding in information theory (KL divergence decomposition)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests across 7 benchmarks spanning vision understanding and hallucination, with 3 model variants, showing consistent improvements and robust ablations validating design choices
Practical data efficiency: Achieves better performance with substantially fewer training tokens (21-65% reduction depending on model), demonstrating the method's practical value
Complementary to existing approaches: Demonstrates orthogonality to inference-time (VCD, PAI, VAR) and training-based methods (LACING), with additive benefits when combined

Strong mechanistic validation: Clear evidence through attention analysis (Fig 4) and text-corruption experiments (Fig 5) that the method genuinely improves visual grounding rather than just optimizing benchmarks
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-structured paper with implementation details, hyperparameters, and qualitative examples enabling reproduction
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution is relatively incremental—applying existing selective training principles (Lin et al. 2024) to LVLMs with a specific metric. The conceptual advance is modest

VIG's validity as ground truth is questionable: Perplexity changes reflect model prediction shifts, not necessarily semantic visual necessity. Blurred image approach for visual absence is an imperfect approximation; alternative visual nulling strategies not explored

Modest improvements across many metrics: LLaVAW 7B (+3.7%), MMVet 13B (+1.9%), DocVQA (+0.2-1.2%), and hallucination metrics show inconsistent gains; some improvements are small relative to typical training variance

Narrow architectural scope: Evaluation limited primarily to LLaVA variants with only one additional model (ShareGPT4V). Generalization to recent architectures (Qwen, DeepSeek, InternVL) unexplored; acknowledged but problematic for ICML submission

Significant computational overhead inadequately analyzed: VIG precomputation takes 6 hours on 8 RTX 4090s; total cost comparison with full-data training is missing. Claims about efficiency don't account for this preprocessing cost

Incomplete design justification: Reusing threshold τ_p at both sample and token levels justified only to avoid hyperparameters, but Table C.1 shows τ_p varies across models. No principled method for practitioners to select τ_p for new models

Missing critical analyses: No investigation of which sample types/domains are disproportionately filtered, no failure case analysis, no human evaluation of grounding quality, no sensitivity to blur parameters
Token-level masking under-analyzed: Computing loss only on selected tokens while maintaining full logits could introduce gradient flow biases; optimization implications not discussed

strengths: Clear problem motivation with concrete examples demonstrating heterogeneous visual dependency in multimodal datasets
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V) and diverse benchmarks covering both vision understanding and hallucination metrics
Thorough analysis including attention allocation studies, text corruption robustness testing, and detailed ablation studies validating design choices
Demonstrated data efficiency gains (34-79% token reduction) with maintained or improved performance
Shows orthogonal improvements when combined with existing visual grounding methods (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: VIG is a straightforward perplexity comparison metric, and selective training directly applies recent LLM techniques; the core contribution is incremental engineering rather than methodological innovation

Questionable technical design choices inadequately justified: (1) Gaussian blur-based visual absence simulation is crude and preserves structural/color information; (2) reusing same threshold τp at sample and token levels lacks empirical or theoretical justification; (3) computing VIG on pre-trained models for instruction-tuning selection ignores potential task mismatch

Modest and inconsistent empirical improvements: many gains are marginal (<1 point on POPE, DocVQA, CHAIR); no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; unclear if improvements are meaningful

Severely limited generalization scope: experiments concentrated almost exclusively on LLaVA-family architectures; only one alternative baseline (ShareGPT4V, which is also LLaVA-based); no evaluation on Qwen, GPT-4V-style models, or non-instruction-tuning domains

Insufficient treatment of computational overhead: VIG scoring requires 6 hours on 8 GPUs; no analysis of total cost (VIG + training) vs. baseline; overhead not properly weighed against efficiency gains, especially for new models/datasets

Analysis limitations: token-level statistics (Table 2) may reflect dataset artifacts rather than genuine visual necessity; attention increase shows correlation but not causation; missing comparison with simpler heuristics (caption length, difficulty-based selection)
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned, no random seed information, varying computational setups (RTX 4090 vs. A100), no statistical significance reporting across runs

Incomplete treatment of limitations and design decisions: no ablation on blur parameters, no justification for p=70 across diverse models, no discussion of negative VIG semantics, limited related work on competing data efficiency approaches

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing language bias in LVLMs with a novel perplexity-based metric (VIG) that is theoretically grounded with clear mathematical derivations
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple models (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B), diverse benchmarks (vision understanding and hallucination evaluation), and thorough ablation studies

Practical and significant data efficiency gains: 30-79% token reduction while maintaining or improving performance across all benchmarks, with particularly strong improvements on hallucination metrics (POPE +5.93%, MMHal +8.47% on 7B)
Demonstrates orthogonality with existing methods, showing complementary benefits when combined with inference-time strategies (VCD, PAI, VAR) and architectural modifications (LACING)

Fine-grained interpretability through token-level decomposition that effectively identifies visually-grounded tokens (colors, spatial relations) versus structural tokens, providing insights into model behavior
Strong reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, explicit thresholds, training data details, and extensive supplementary results enabling verification
weaknesses: Limited architectural diversity: evaluation restricted to LLaVA-1.5 and ShareGPT4V families; generalization to other LVLM architectures (Qwen-VL, LLaVA-NeXT, etc.) remains unclear and is acknowledged only as future work

Computational overhead of VIG scoring insufficiently explored: requires ~6 hours for 665K samples; total wall-clock time comparison with baseline training not provided; may be prohibitive for resource-constrained practitioners despite one-time reusability claim

Visual absence simulation via Gaussian blur is an approximation without rigorous validation: no ablation on blur strategies, no analysis of residual signals in blurred images, limited justification for why blur specifically simulates visual information loss

Modest or inconsistent improvements on specific benchmarks: DocVQA gains minimal (+0.20-1.19), MMBench improvements marginal (0.87% for 7B), CHAIR metrics show mixed patterns; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported

Design choices insufficiently justified: using same threshold τ_p for sample and token selection is convenient but potentially suboptimal; choice of p=70 not deeply motivated; no exploration of separate thresholds or adaptive selection schemes

Limited analysis of failure modes: unclear why random sampling degrades performance, what fraction of samples have ambiguous VIG scores, when VIG misidentifies important samples, or which task/domain categories are problematic

Small benchmark for key evaluation: LLaVAW uses only 24 images across 60 questions, limiting reliability of assessment; no cross-dataset validation (train on one dataset's selected samples, test on another)

strengths: Well-grounded theoretical foundation with rigorous mathematical derivations connecting VIG to perplexity, cross-entropy loss, and KL divergence
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple architectures (4 model families) and extensive benchmarks covering both vision understanding and hallucination evaluation
Consistent performance improvements across all tested models with significant data efficiency gains (34-79% token reduction while maintaining or improving performance)
Excellent empirical analysis validating that VIG aligns with benchmark-level modality dependencies and successfully identifies visually grounded tokens vs. function words
Strong reproducibility with comprehensive implementation details, hyperparameters, training configurations, and honest discussion of computational overhead
Practical utility: architecture-agnostic approach requiring no model modifications and adding no inference overhead; demonstrates orthogonality to existing methods
Thorough ablation studies examining selection levels and ratios, with analysis of data distribution preservation showing long-tail concept retention
weaknesses: Visual absence simulation via Gaussian blur lacks sufficient justification; blur preserves spatial/structural information, and no empirical validation that it truly represents visual absence within the model's processing
Modest improvements on several benchmarks reduce practical significance (e.g., MMBench +0.87, DocVQA +0.20 for LLaVA-1.5 7B); no error bars or statistical significance testing reported

Hyperparameter choices appear pragmatic rather than principled: selection of p=70 lacks clear justification, and reusing τ_p at both sample/token levels is framed as avoiding hyperparameters rather than principled design
Limited architectural scope with experiments primarily on LLaVA-family models; generalization to recent architectures with different alignment strategies remains unclear
Computational overhead of VIG scoring (6 hours on 8 RTX 4090s) is non-negligible and could limit adoption, though framed as one-time cost; total cost-benefit analysis incomplete
Technical limitations: decomposition in Eq. 6 assumes token-level independence despite autoregressive dependencies; text-only samples left unchanged means method doesn't optimize this component
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-seed experiments reported; absence of direct comparisons with other data selection/valuation methods

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing language bias in LVLMs with clear articulation of the issue
Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple architectures (4 LVLM variants) and diverse benchmarks (vision understanding + hallucination)
Solid theoretical grounding for VIG metric through reformulation in terms of cross-entropy loss and KL divergence
Extensive ablation studies and supplementary analysis including attention analysis, text-reliance evaluation, and data distribution effects
Consistent improvements across virtually all tested benchmarks, demonstrating robustness
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters and implementation details provided
weaknesses: Fundamental methodological concern: Using blurred images to simulate visual absence is crude and lacks empirical validation that it adequately removes semantic visual information, potentially confounding VIG measurements
Incremental core contribution: Measuring information contribution via loss differences is established; selective training is a straightforward application of this principle
Computational overhead inadequately addressed: ~6 hours VIG computation adds ~86% to total training cost, but cost-benefit analysis is missing or minimized

Task distribution shift confound: Filtering heavily removes text-dominant tasks (GQA: 44.2% retention) while keeping vision tasks (OCR-VQA: 98.4%), making it unclear whether improvements come from VIG principle or from task distribution shift alone
Modest empirical improvements: Many benchmarks show 2-4% gains (DocVQA only +0.20%, MMBench +0.87%); larger hallucination improvements may be artifacts of distribution shift

Design choices lack justification: Reusing threshold τp for both sample and token levels is heuristic; p=70 selection ratio appears arbitrary with no principled selection method; same-threshold choice not ablated
Missing theoretical justification: While VIG is motivated, there is no theoretical explanation for why training on high-VIG samples should improve visual grounding beyond intuition
Limited novelty in selective training approach: General selective/curriculum learning and data pruning are well-established; positioning relative to this literature is unclear
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Most comparisons are against inference-time methods; limited comparison with other data-centric approaches
Key ablation missing: Cannot separate effects of VIG-based filtering from effects of task-distribution shift, which is critical for validating the core claim

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 model architectures and 8 benchmarks with consistent improvements; significant practical efficiency gains (LLaVA-1.5 13B achieves better performance with 79% fewer tokens)

Well-motivated problem addressing language bias in LVLMs with intuitive solution; clear mathematical formulation with proper theoretical grounding (perplexity-based metric reformulated in cross-entropy and KL divergence terms)

Thorough empirical validation of core claims: VIG alignment with visual grounding degree (Table 1), benchmark modality dependency (Figure 2), token-level decomposition identifying visually salient words via POS analysis (Figure 4)

Solid experimental design with proper ablations (selection levels, ratios), data distribution analysis preserving long-tail concepts, qualitative examples, and maintenance of text-only performance; demonstrates orthogonality to existing methods (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING)

Addresses important real problem: heterogeneous multimodal datasets containing both text-answerable and visually-grounded examples; practical method without architectural modifications or inference overhead
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: applies straightforward perplexity-based importance weighting (existing technique) to selective training; core contribution is engineering-focused rather than providing new insights into visual grounding or multimodal learning

Visual absence simulation via Gaussian blur is methodologically questionable: blurred images may retain high-level information and are not equivalent to true visual absence; lacks justification for blur hyperparameters and no comparison with alternatives (text-only models, different degradation patterns); this is a critical choice deserving deeper analysis

Threshold selection lacks principled justification: fixed p=70 appears arbitrary; models show different VIG distributions requiring different thresholds (Table D.1: -0.021 to 0.046), suggesting approach may not be fully principled; using identical threshold τp for sample-level and token-level selection conflates two distinct problems

Missing statistical significance testing: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported; improvements are sometimes marginal (MMBench +0.87, POPE CS +0.03 for LLaVA-1.5 7B); results appear to be from single runs, limiting reliability claims

Theoretical gap: assumes deterministic supervision (Dirac delta), but many VQA datasets have multiple valid answers; impact of this simplification on interpretation and performance not discussed; incomplete handling of when/why VIG signal is reliable

Limited architectural and dataset diversity: most experiments on LLaVA/ShareGPT4V with similar instruction-tuning paradigms; Open-Qwen2VL is encouraging but insufficient; no evaluation on recent diverse architectures (DeepSeek-VL, newer Qwen variants); limits generality claims

Incomplete analysis of method limitations: no discussion of failure modes, sample types where VIG misleads, or sensitivity to hyperparameters; computational overhead (~6 hours for VIG calculation on 8 RTX 4090s) may be prohibitive for large-scale applications; scaling behavior not discussed

Some marginal improvements and design choices: POPE CS improvement of +0.03 and CHAIR degradation in some cases; using same threshold for both selection levels is convenient but likely suboptimal; LACING+VIG outperforms VIG alone on MMBench (67.89 vs 66.33), raising questions about relative importance
